{"id": "66:6/q31", "question": "How is مَآ أَمَرَهُمْ parsed?", "turns_on": "Relative pronoun with an omitted link versus verbal noun or apposition.", "positions": [{"id": "66:6/q31/p1", "position": "ما is relative, with an omitted preposition or returning pronoun: what He commanded them concerning.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās says a relative ما loses its return pronoun; al-Samīn reconstructs ما أمرهم به, with an accusative gap after preposition loss. Abū Ḥayyān also gives an omitted preposition. Al-Kashshāf gives 'in what He commands', comparing 20:93."}, {"id": "66:6/q31/p2", "position": "ما is a verbal noun or apposition expressing God's command.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās says no return pronoun is needed; al-Samīn takes an inclusive apposition to God's name, لا يعصون أمره. Al-Kashshāf and Abū Ḥayyān compare an accusative appositive and 20:93; Bursevī calls it a supplement."}, {"id": "66:6/q31/p3", "position": "The clause is an adjective in nominative position.", "reasons": "Al-Nasafī says لا يعصون الله is a nominative adjective clause and ما أمرهم an accusative substitute."}]}
{"id": "66:6/q32", "question": "What does the angels' obedience imply about their moral status and duties?", "turns_on": "Moral assignment and grace, delight, or innate cosmological subjection.", "positions": [{"id": "66:6/q32/p1", "position": "Angels are charged with divine commands and protected from disobedience.", "reasons": "Rāzī says the verse shows angels are morally tasked in the afterlife and defines disobedience as violating command or prohibition; al-Riḍā says God's grace protects angels from disbelief and disgraceful acts. Bursevī reports a view that heavenly angels are intellects without competing appetite or desire; it distinguishes angels who never descend and those who never ascend."}, {"id": "66:6/q32/p2", "position": "Obeying God's command is itself the angels' delight.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī attributes this to some Muʿtazilites, comparing it with the delight of Paradise's inhabitants."}, {"id": "66:6/q32/p3", "position": "Angels as celestial powers obey innately because they are subject to divine overpowering.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī says their obedience enables their influence in terrestrial affairs; Asad relates angelic obedience to the spiritual and material law of cause and effect."}]}
{"id": "66:6/q33", "question": "Can God impose duties in the future, including on angels?", "turns_on": "The theological possibility of future divine obligation.", "positions": [{"id": "66:6/q33/p1", "position": "God can impose duties today or tomorrow and charge angels as He wills.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī calls this the view of the people of truth and expressly rejects the opposing Muʿtazilite doctrine."}, {"id": "66:6/q33/p2", "position": "Imposing a duty tomorrow is impossible.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī reports this as the Muʿtazilite claim and rejects it."}]}
{"id": "66:6/q34", "question": "Do heavenly angels earn reward for avoiding prohibitions?", "turns_on": "Whether refraining is available as a duty and whether it needs intention for reward.", "positions": [{"id": "66:6/q34/p1", "position": "These heavenly angels have no prohibitions to avoid and thus lack reward for refraining.", "reasons": "Bursevī transmits a distinction from humans and earthly angels, who can earn both by obeying commands and avoiding prohibitions."}, {"id": "66:6/q34/p2", "position": "Abstention earns reward only if intended as obedience, though no intention is needed merely to avoid liability.", "reasons": "Al-Kirmānī distinguishes intended refraining from merely not committing a sin, illustrated by leaving fornication."}]}
{"id": "66:6/q35", "question": "How are masculine forms used with angels?", "turns_on": "Grammatical freedom of the broken plural and the rhetorical weight assigned to gender forms.", "positions": [{"id": "66:6/q35/p1", "position": "Nominal descriptions, commands to angels, and verbs of their worship are masculine.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī surveys descriptors such as المقرّبون, باسطو أيديهم, مسوّمين, مردفين and منزلين; commands اسجدوا, أنبئوني, فقعوا; and verbs of entering, witnessing and glorifying. He says masculine worship is fuller and recalls male messengers. He contrasts angelic glad tidings, whose forms are feminine, and notes a broken plural may take either gender."}, {"id": "66:6/q35/p2", "position": "A broken plural permits both masculine and feminine agreement.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī compares masculine angel agreement in Ṣād with feminine agreement in Āl ʿImrān, citing 38:73 and 3:39."}, {"id": "66:6/q35/p3", "position": "Masculine forms suit greater breadth of worship and stronger punishment.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī contrasts masculine oath response and lam with a narrower feminine verb and qad, and compares harsh punishment forms in 8:50, 47:27, 25:25, 41:30 and 97:4."}]}
{"id": "66:6/q36", "question": "What inward lesson is drawn from protecting oneself and one's family?", "turns_on": "Whether family is a spiritual bond, a field of ethical training, or an image of inner powers.", "positions": [{"id": "66:6/q36/p1", "position": "Purify worldly attachment and choose pure companions, since love binds souls together.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī says attachment to impure people or natural faculties drags one into an abyss, while loving saints gathers one with them under the report that people are resurrected with those they love. Bursevī transmits this and another allusion: a leader's lapse becomes followers' lapse, so purification can help household members follow."}, {"id": "66:6/q36/p2", "position": "Accept admonition, model worship, follow the Sunna, and cultivate character within the household.", "reasons": "Al-Sulamī transmits Ibn ʿAṭāʾ on accepting counsel, Abū ʿUthmān on acting on admonition, and Abū al-Ḥasan al-Warrāq on duties and Prophetic practices; al-Qushayrī adds example, Sunna, community and good character."}, {"id": "66:6/q36/p3", "position": "The spiritual Fire is distance from God, fueled by lower selves and hardened hearts.", "reasons": "Al-Taʾwīlāt al-Najmiyya says intellectual believers must guard against expulsion after neglecting the primordial covenant; al-Qāshānī speaks of divine overpowering of desire-entangled souls."}]}
{"id": "66:6/q37", "question": "What is reported about the severity of the Fire itself?", "turns_on": "Terrifying punishment and promised reward in the associated reports.", "positions": [{"id": "66:6/q37/p1", "position": "Its torment permits no rest, sleep, comfort, or excuse.", "reasons": "Al-Sulamī attributes this warning to Yaḥyā, adding that even iron could not withstand the Fire."}, {"id": "66:6/q37/p2", "position": "A family that fulfills its duties may be gathered together in Paradise.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj reports this hadith; similar reports in al-Kashshāf, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Bursevī, Ālūsī and Elmalılı urge prayer, fasting, alms and care for poor, orphans and neighbors."}]}
{"id": "66:6/q38", "question": "How does this verse connect with the surah's surrounding passage?", "turns_on": "The direction of the passage's shift and the verses used to explain family responsibility.", "positions": [{"id": "66:6/q38/p1", "position": "The Prophet's household episode broadens into a warning to all believers to reform themselves and their families.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān, Biqāʿī, Ibn ʿĀshūr, Iṣlāḥī and Kuran Yolu trace the move from the Prophet and wives to all Muslims. Ibn ʿĀshūr says believers are accompanied by the Prophet in admonishing even when advice hurts; Biqāʿī says the wives' earlier warning preserves respect and their virtues reflect good upbringing."}, {"id": "66:6/q38/p2", "position": "The passage alternates warnings and commands to believers, unbelievers and the Prophet.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī traces protection, the unbelievers' inability to excuse themselves at 66:7, repentance at 66:8 and struggle at 66:9; Elmalılı notes the turn to unbelievers. Study Quran describes the passage from wives (1–5) through family duty (6), unbelievers (7) and opponents (9)."}, {"id": "66:6/q38/p3", "position": "The surah repeatedly vindicates the Prophet before disclosing the dispute involving his wives.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī says shifts among the Prophet, believers and wives reveal the episode only after divine support is secured."}, {"id": "66:6/q38/p4", "position": "Its command to family parallels 20:132 and 26:214, and more generally 5:2.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī and al-Kiyā connect family prayer and warning nearest kin to 20:132 and 26:214; al-Qurṭubī also invokes cooperation in righteousness in 5:2."}]}
{"id": "66:6/q39", "question": "What is distinctive about believers being told to protect themselves?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "66:6/q39/p1", "position": "Here believers are directly told to shield themselves; elsewhere they ask God to protect them.", "reasons": "Study Quran compares prayers in 3:16, 3:191 and 40:7."}]}
{"id": "66:6/q40", "question": "What date and classification are given for the surah?", "turns_on": "Whether all twelve verses or only the first nine are Medinan.", "positions": [{"id": "66:6/q40/p1", "position": "It is Medinan, probably around 7 AH.", "reasons": "Asad places it in the second half of the Medinan period; Study Quran says likely 7/629."}, {"id": "66:6/q40/p2", "position": "A minority counts verses 1–9 as Medinan and the last three as Makkan.", "reasons": "Study Quran reports this alternative."}]}
{"id": "66:6/q41", "question": "What alternate title is reported for the surah?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "66:6/q41/p1", "position": "Sūrat al-Nabī, 'the Sūrah of the Prophet'.", "reasons": "Asad cites al-Zamakhsharī; the title reflects the first half's concern with the Prophet's personal and family life."}]}

{"id": "66:6/q43", "question": "What account of the written Quran and its transmission appears in the cited material?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "66:6/q43/p1", "position": "The companions collected the Quran from writing and memory and transmitted the revelation entrusted to them.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr defines ʿasab as immature palm-frond material through al-Jawharī and likhāf as flat stone writing pieces. Zayd gathered palm stems, stone pieces and memorized passages. Ibn Kathīr says the Prophet's full delivery is attested at ʿArafāt and by orders to convey even one verse; writing non-Quranic material was restrained to prevent confusion, not to stop Sunna transmission. He says no revealed Quran was lost; Abū Bakr's sheets passed through ʿUmar and Ḥafṣa to ʿUthmān."}]}
{"id": "67:22/q01", "question": "How does the opening question advance the preceding argument?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "67:22/q01/p1", "position": "It forces recognition that the upright walker is better guided and that the two states are unequal.", "reasons": "Bursevi and Alusi say the interrogative hamza leads the conjunction in wording though the logical order is reversed. Ibn Ashur makes the fa a consequence of the preceding signs and calls for acknowledgment. Tabataba'i says the obstinate are distanced from direct address. Ibn Ashur rejects an evenhanded reading like 34:24 because this context argues and proves; Biqai says the deniers' physical route knowledge contrasts with their failure on the spiritual road."}]}
{"id": "67:22/q02", "question": "What does mukibban or akabba mean, and how does its form work?", "turns_on": "Whether the hamza is a regular reflexive or passive marker, marks entering a state, or also occurs in transitive usage.", "positions": [{"id": "67:22/q02/p1", "position": "Akabba means to become bent or prone, entering a state; mukibb is a person bent or fallen face-down.", "reasons": "Kashshaf denies that Form IV is a regular passive and cites infaḍḍa, alʾama and qashʿa/aqshaʿ; inkabba and inqashaʿa are the regular reflexives. Baydawi and Alusi agree. Abu Hayyan and the Shaykh say the hamza marks entering a state; Ibn Ashur calls mukibb the active participle. Razi reports Kashshaf. Samin reports Zamakhshari and the Shaykh, but criticizes the Shaykh's attack as borrowed and quotes a poet. Abu Hayyan disputes Zamakhshari's categorical denial of responsive afʿala using Sibawayh and cites Ibn Maʿzuz's critique. Tabataba'i reports Zamakhshari. Bursevi glosses it as fallen face-down."}, {"id": "67:22/q02/p2", "position": "Akabba is the intransitive or reflexive counterpart of transitive kabba, an exceptional reversal of the usual Form IV pattern.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba distinguishes akabba with alif from kabba without it. Tabari cites al-Aʿsha's fallen camel digging at its sides. Wahidi gives 'he cast him down, so he fell'; Ibn Atiyya cites the Prophet's 'harvest of tongues' for transitive kabba and compares qashaʿa/aqshaʿa. Jishumi explicitly calls this unusual and compares cloud dispersal; Razi reports Wahidi's account. Tabataba'i also gives the transitive 'cast down' gloss. Kashshaf and Baydawi reject treating it as a regular passive."}, {"id": "67:22/q02/p3", "position": "Akabbahu can itself be transitive, like kabbahu.", "reasons": "Alusi reports Ibn al-Aʿrabi's lexical evidence and says this usage removes the apparent irregularity."}]}
{"id": "67:22/q03", "question": "What is the grammatical role of mukibban?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "67:22/q03/p1", "position": "It is a circumstantial accusative describing the walker.", "reasons": "Samin says it modifies the subject of yamshi; Abu Hayyan derives it from intransitive akabba. Alusi likewise places it in the relative clause; Bursevi adds that the walker stumbles repeatedly on rough ground with impaired strength."}]}
{"id": "67:22/q04", "question": "Whom do the two walkers represent?", "turns_on": "Whether the images are a general religious parable, a report about named people, a blind/sighted illustration, or a further application.", "positions": [{"id": "67:22/q04/p1", "position": "They represent the unbeliever or polytheist and the believer or monotheist generally.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Dahhak supply the general parable in Tabari, Jishumi, Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan. Muqatil adds blindness of heart versus Muhammad's pure heart, also reporting a specific identification. Wahidi, Baghawi and Qurtubi connect disbelief's blindness with Islam's visible road. Baydawi, Biqai and Alusi describe two religious ways; Ibn Ashur explicitly assigns the first to idolaters and the second to believers, citing divided tribal gods, Joseph 12:39, and 6:153. Tabataba'i says the believer seeks truth with insight; Kuranyolu adds Satan's false paths; Study Quran notes immediate desires. Ibn Ashur says an unassigned reading weakens the warning and could reverse its target."}, {"id": "67:22/q04/p2", "position": "The pair is Abu Jahl and Muhammad.", "reasons": "Muqatil, al-Kalbi, Ibn Abbas and others are reported by Wahidi, Ibn Atiyya, Razi, Qurtubi, Nasafi, Abu Hayyan and Ibn Ashur; Kashshaf's Kalbi report names the Messenger. Muqatil contrasts Abu Jahl's blindness of heart and Muhammad's pure heart."}, {"id": "67:22/q04/p3", "position": "The pair is Abu Jahl and Hamza ibn Abd al-Muttalib.", "reasons": "Wahidi gives Ata from Ibn Abbas; Ibn Atiyya attributes it to occasion-of-revelation transmitters; Razi, Abu Hayyan and Alusi also cite this identification. Kashshaf and Qurtubi report Hamza as an alternate upright person."}, {"id": "67:22/q04/p4", "position": "The pair is Abu Jahl and Ammar ibn Yasir.", "reasons": "Mawardi, Wahidi, Razi and Qurtubi attribute this to Ikrima."}, {"id": "67:22/q04/p5", "position": "The upright walker is Abu Bakr, opposite Abu Jahl.", "reasons": "Qurtubi reports this alternative without naming a transmitter; Ibn Ashur lists it among reported identifications."}, {"id": "67:22/q04/p6", "position": "The contrast can represent a blind person and a sighted person.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba, Kashshaf, Razi, Qurtubi, Baydawi, Bursevi and Alusi use blindness and sight as the physical model. Kashshaf says it represents unbeliever and believer; Alusi says the image can still illustrate the broader comparison."}, {"id": "67:22/q04/p7", "position": "The contrast is the self bent toward sensual desire versus one following Islam or the path of unity.", "reasons": "Tustari says innate desire deprives the first of divine guidance and makes the second a follower of Islamic laws and prophetic models. Qashani points to the lower realm and natural attractions versus a path of unity whose full measure cannot be attained."}, {"id": "67:22/q04/p8", "position": "By application, the verse distinguishes opponents of Ali's authority from his followers.", "reasons": "Tabataba'i reports traditions of this application and says it is not the direct interpretation."}]}
{"id": "67:22/q05", "question": "What physical scene explains the face-down walker and his opposite?", "turns_on": "The commentators supply different physical pictures and degrees of metaphor for the same contrast.", "positions": [{"id": "67:22/q05/p1", "position": "A stumbling traveler on rough or crooked ground is contrasted with one walking steadily on a level, straight road.", "reasons": "Tabari, Mawardi and Qurtubi say the first cannot see ahead or sideways. Kashshaf and Razi mention repeated falls on uneven ground; Razi separately mentions confused wandering. Baydawi and Nasafi describe safe steady walking on an even road. Biqai adds desire, ignorance, repeated hardship, and the upright traveler's raised head and prepared broad road. Tabataba'i says the first misses rises, dips, hazards and destination. Alusi and Bursevi repeat the uneven route. Kuranyolu asks which reaches the goal safely."}, {"id": "67:22/q05/p2", "position": "A blind person gropes, unable to see the road, while a sighted person can follow it.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba names blindness, as Ibn Jawzi also reports; Tha'labi says heart and eyes are blind; Jishumi says the first cannot distinguish truth from falsehood. Kashshaf, Razi, Qurtubi, Baydawi, Bursevi and Alusi give this as an alternative model. Bursevi cites a Persian couplet contrasting certainty and blind guesswork. Asad likens immediate worldly fixation to an earthworm."}, {"id": "67:22/q05/p3", "position": "The first traveler bends close to the ground to search tracks on winding side routes; the second confidently uses a clear main road.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says the face-down posture represents the polytheist's uncertain search among tribal gods and for beneficial power, whereas one Lord gives the believer confidence. He calls the description three layered representational metaphors."}, {"id": "67:22/q05/p4", "position": "The fallen person is immersed in error, ignorance or lower desire rather than literally navigating ground.", "reasons": "Mujahid and Ibn Abbas give error versus guidance; Wahidi's Kalbi likens following one's own head to a beast. Jishumi adds inability to tell truth from falsehood; Biqai says desire prevents seeing signs or hearing counsel. Elmalili likens low fixation to crawling animals; Asad to an earthworm. Islahi says enslavement to desire misses the goal."}]}

state made visible in the future.", "positions": [{"id": "67:22/q06/p1", "position": "It is a parable for guidance and error in worldly life.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya says the first three identifications are figurative and contrasts them with Qatada's literal afterlife view. Abu Hayyan attributes the worldly metaphor to Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Dahhak. Ibn Ashur argues it depicts the truth of the two creeds here."}, {"id": "67:22/q06/p2", "position": "The unbeliever literally walks or is gathered face-down at Resurrection, while the believer goes upright.", "reasons": "Qatada repeatedly says worldly disobedience leads to being raised on the face and obedience to upright resurrection. The Prophet answers that the Creator of foot-walking can enable face-walking. Wahidi cites 17:97, Study Quran 25:34, and Ibn Kathir 37:22–26. Baydawi and Bursevi give the destinations as Fire and Paradise; Alusi says this reading is no parable."}, {"id": "67:22/q06/p3", "position": "The worldly spiritual condition becomes a corresponding visible state in the next life.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya says disbelievers undergo both states. Ibn Kathir applies the contrast in both lives and cites 37:22–26; Biqai and Bursevi say hidden states are disclosed at Resurrection. Elmalili says the animal-like crawl continues in Hell."}]}
{"id": "67:22/q07", "question": "What report explains how someone can walk on his face?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "67:22/q07/p1", "position": "The Prophet says the One who made people walk on their feet can make them walk on their faces.", "reasons": "The reports vary between 'people' and 'the unbeliever' and between making him walk in the next world and raising him there. Abd al-Razzaq, Tabari, Zajjaj, Ibn Atiyya, Abu Hayyan, Ibn Kathir, Bursevi and Alusi relay it; Ibn Kathir names Anas as transmitter. Qatada uses it in support of the literal Resurrection reading."}]}
{"id": "67:22/q08", "question": "What does ahda mean in this comparison?", "turns_on": "Whether the form compares two degrees of guidance or names guidance where the other party has none.", "positions": [{"id": "67:22/q08/p1", "position": "It is a comparative of guidance: the upright traveler is more rightly guided.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya calls it the comparative of huda; Abu Hayyan says every listener would answer for the upright walker. Nasafi and Burhan give the implied answer. Biqai and Bursevi say a level route can be found by chance, so real guidance requires discernment. Jishumi says the upright walker knows the way. Damghani links just upright walking with guidance."}, {"id": "67:22/q08/p2", "position": "It means 'guided' in superlative form without a real comparison, since the first walker has no guidance.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says ahda refers to knowing the road, cites a similar noncomparative reading of 12:33, and allows mockery or light irony."}]}
{"id": "67:22/q09", "question": "How are the two man clauses and ahda joined?", "turns_on": "Whether a single predicate serves both alternatives or one or both descriptions require ellipsis.", "positions": [{"id": "67:22/q09/p1", "position": "The first man is subject and ahda its predicate; the second man is coordinated and needs no separate predicate.", "reasons": "Nahhas, Samin, Alusi and Ibn Ashur give this syntax; Samin uses 'Is Zayd standing, or Amr?' to show that am asks between two things under one predicate. Ibn Ashur says both man forms are relative pronouns."}, {"id": "67:22/q09/p2", "position": "The second man has an omitted predicate supplied from ahda.", "reasons": "Samin reports Abu al-Baqa's analysis; Samin argues against its need, and Nasafi also states that ahda licenses an omitted predicate."}, {"id": "67:22/q09/p3", "position": "Each half of the paired comparison omits a counterpart supplied by the other.", "reasons": "Burhan says the full comparative has four elements; each description supplies what the other leaves implicit, and the answer favors the upright walker."}]}
{"id": "67:22/q10", "question": "How is amman read or written here?", "turns_on": "One note concerns Talha's pronunciation; Burhan explains the joined written form.", "positions": [{"id": "67:22/q10/p1", "position": "Talha reads am man with an ungeminated mim.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya reports Talha's reading."}, {"id": "67:22/q10/p2", "position": "The written amman is joined because the two walkers form one comparison without separate subcategories.", "reasons": "Burhan compares joined am man in 27:61. He explains that an ma is separated when 'what' contains real subcategories with different rulings and says mimman is always joined because conceptual distinctions do not split actual entities."}]}
{"id": "67:22/q11", "question": "What does sawiyyan describe?", "turns_on": "Whether sawiyy is explained as bodily uprightness or the moral guidance that posture signifies.", "positions": [{"id": "67:22/q11/p1", "position": "It means fully upright, even or sound in walking.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur calls it an active-participle form and cites 19:43; Tabari, Nasafi and Biqai contrast posture and level movement."}, {"id": "67:22/q11/p2", "position": "It can mean just or rightly guided.", "reasons": "Damghani gives 'just or upright' and cites 20:135; Ibn Jawzi's Nuzha reports the exegetical gloss 'guided'."}]}
{"id": "67:22/q12", "question": "What is the straight path in the verse?", "turns_on": "The expression can denote the road within the image or the religious way represented by that road.", "positions": [{"id": "67:22/q12/p1", "position": "It is a clear, uncrooked and passable road in the travel image.", "reasons": "Tabari says it lacks crookedness; Mawardi says the traveler does not stray. Jishumi, Nasafi, Biqai and Alusi stress clarity, evenness and safety."}, {"id": "67:22/q12/p2", "position": "It signifies the truth or Islam as the believer's religious course.", "reasons": "Mujahid calls it upright truth; Wahidi reports Ibn Abbas, Kalbi, Muqatil, Mujahid and Dahhak naming Islam. Muqatil, Tustari, Wahidi and Qurtubi mention faith, law or prophetic models. Biqai links it to accepting God and original nature free of desire, anger and self-interest. Elmalili specifies tawhid, ethics and sacred law."}, {"id": "67:22/q12/p3", "position": "In an inward reading it is the perfectly straight path of unity.", "reasons": "Qashani says its entire nature and measure cannot be reached or estimated."}]}
{"id": "67:22/q13", "question": "What variant pronunciations of sirat are noted?", "turns_on": "Pronunciation of the initial consonant; the notes say the meaning does not change.", "positions": [{"id": "67:22/q13/p1", "position": "The canonical ishmam gives sad a slight zay sound.", "reasons": "Qiraat-ER says the intermediate pronunciation preserves a trace of the word's non-Arabic origin, between sin and sad."}, {"id": "67:22/q13/p2", "position": "Qalun from Nafi reads it with sin.", "reasons": "Qiraat-ER says this is closer to its stated Latin strāta source and makes no semantic difference."}]}
{"id": "67:22/q14", "question": "Why is no path named for the face-down walker?", "turns_on": "Whether the silence disparages the first route as no path or economizes the paired contrast.", "positions": [{"id": "67:22/q14/p1", "position": "His crooked route scarcely deserves to be called a path.", "reasons": "Baydawi, Biqai, Bursevi's cited 'author of correspondences,' and Alusi give this reason; Biqai stresses that repeated stumbling does not deter him."}, {"id": "67:22/q14/p2", "position": "The second road's straightness supplies the first road's unstated crookedness by contrast.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says the contrast is clear without stating the first road's quality. Biqai calls the paired omissions a rhetorical figure that displays the criminal's worst and the Muslim's best feature; Burhan says each half supplies the other's missing element."}]}
{"id": "67:22/q15", "question": "What broader lesson is drawn from the two ways?", "turns_on": "Whether the reader draws chiefly a spiritual choice or also a concrete ethic for physical roads.", "positions": [{"id": "67:22/q15/p1", "position": "Insight, obedience and monotheism guide a person toward the true goal; desire and ignorance make one stray.", "reasons": "Wahidi's Kalbi describes animal-like headlong following of one's own head. {"id": "67:22/q16", "question": "What report about hearts is applied to this verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "67:22/q16/p1", "position": "A four-hearts report assigns the inverted heart to the polytheist and recites the face-down verse.", "reasons": "Tabataba'i cites Abu Ja'far in al-Kafi: a bright lamp-like heart belongs to the grateful and patient believer, a sealed heart to the hypocrite, an inverted heart to the polytheist, and a fourth combines faith and hypocrisy. {"id": "68:1/q05", "question": "Why does the sūra open with نٓ?", "turns_on": "Its relation to the sūra's argument, the status of disjoint letters, and whether phonetic, symbolic, or reported referents are intended.", "positions": [{"id": "68:1/q05/p1", "position": "The familiar letters challenge hearers to match the Qurʾān made from their own alphabet.", "reasons": "Abū Muslim and Bint al-Shāṭiʾ connect the letter to inimitability; she stresses the early dispute over 'tales of the ancients' and the first revelation's Read and Pen. {"id": "68:1/q06", "question": "What happened in reports about the primordial Pen and the fish?", "turns_on": "Different report chains, the order of creation, cosmological details, names and the status of literal versus interpretive readings.", "positions": [{"id": "68:1/q06/p1", "position": "God first created the Pen, ordered it to write destiny, then created the fish, spread earth upon it and steadied its movement with mountains.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās versions vary on whether water vapor forms heaven before or after the fish and whether the fish is above water or below the seventh earth; some explicitly recite 68:1–2. Ibn ʿĀshūr describes actual lines on pages."}, {"id": "68:1/q11/p5", "position": "What people know or do.", "reasons": "Separate Ibn ʿAbbās glosses give knowledge and deeds/actions rather than a named written text."}, {"id": "68:1/q11/p6", "position": "Ancient legends copied by Arab opponents.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ argues the wording anticipates 68:15 and cites claims in 25:5, 6:25, 8:31, 27:68, 16:24, 46:17 and 83:13."}, {"id": "68:1/q11/p7", "position": "Beneficial writing God undertakes for people and lands.", "reasons": "ʿUmar ibn Wāṣil describes an encompassing divine record of welfare."}]}
{"id": "68:1/q12", "question": "What does يَسْطُرُونَ mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the gloss names the basic lexical action, an interpretive extension, or the verb's continuing aspect.", "positions": [{"id": "68:1/q12/p1", "position": "They write, specifically forming lines or rows of writing.", "reasons": "Ruʾba's poem witnesses saṭr as writing for Majāz and Ṭabarī; Jishumī gives suṭūr and asṭur as plurals. Samarāʾī contrasts saṭr's extended lines with kataba's possible single letter or word."}, {"id": "68:1/q12/p2", "position": "It can extend to doing or knowing.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās is reported separately with both glosses; these are interpretive extensions beyond the usual lexical 'write'."}, {"id": "68:1/q12/p3", "position": "Its imperfective form covers present and future writing.", "reasons": "Elmalılı says Turkish cannot fully carry this aspect and emphasizes that the Highest Pen's inscription continues."}]}
